title: The Outsiders | William Thorndike | Talks at Google
description:
What makes a successful CEO? Most people call to mind a familiar definition: “a seasoned manager with deep industry expertise.” Others might point to the qualities of today’s so-called celebrity CEOs—charisma, virtuoso communication skills, and a confident management style. But what really matters when you run an organization? What is the hallmark of exceptional CEO performance? Quite simply, it is the returns for the shareholders of that company over the long term.

In this refreshing, counterintuitive book, author Will Thorndike brings to bear the analytical wisdom of a successful career in investing, closely evaluating the performance of companies and their leaders. You will meet eight individualistic CEOs whose firms’ average returns outperformed the S&P 500 by a factor of twenty—in other words, an investment of $10,000 with each of these CEOs, on average, would have been worth over $1.5 million twenty-five years later. You may not know all their names, but you will recognize their companies: General Cinema, Ralston Purina, The Washington Post Company, Berkshire Hathaway, General Dynamics, Capital Cities Broadcasting, TCI, and Teledyne. In The Outsiders, you’ll learn the traits and methods—striking for their consistency and relentless rationality—that helped these unique leaders achieve such exceptional performance.

Humble, unassuming, and often frugal, these “outsiders” shunned Wall Street and the press, and shied away from the hottest new management trends. Instead, they shared specific traits that put them and the companies they led on winning trajectories: a laser-sharp focus on per share value as opposed to earnings or sales growth; an exceptional talent for allocating capital and human resources; and the belief that cash flow, not reported earnings, determines a company’s long-term value.

Drawing on years of research and experience, Thorndike tells eye-opening stories, extracting lessons and revealing a compelling alternative model for anyone interested
summary: This talk argues that successful 'outsider' CEOs often prioritize long-term per-share value creation and recurring free cash flow over traditional short-term metrics. The speaker highlights that these leaders, whether through internal growth or strategic acquisitions, frequently employ capital allocation strategies that differ from industry norms to build durable competitive advantages. While some companies like Amazon and Google are praised for their high-return internal growth, others like Oracle are noted for using acquisitions as a primary channel, and the speaker suggests that standard financial metrics may not always apply to these unique business models.

claims.claim: American Tower is a dominant public company in the cell tower business that has built its business well, focusing on metrics like tower cash flow and EBITDA.
claims.quote: American Tower is the largest player and, historically, if you sit at one of their presentations, they'll talk about number of towers, revenue, what they call tower cash flow, and EBITDA, which is the use of the metric of cash flow that they talk about.
claims.speaker: William Thorndike

claims.claim: Crown Castle evolved to optimize for recurring free cash flow per share, a single metric differentiated from industry peers, indicating strong value creation potential.
claims.quote: And evolved over time, but eventually, they would just say, we're running our business to optimize for one thing and that's recurring free cash flow per share. And so they had moved to a single metric that was differentiated from what others in the industry were doing.
claims.speaker: William Thorndike

claims.claim: Jeff Bezos is considered a fascinating outsider CEO who optimizes for per share values 5 to 10 years out due to his large ownership concentration.
claims.quote: And I believe he's optimizing for per share values 5 to 10 years out. And he can afford that time frame because he owns such a large percentage of the company himself. So he has the ability to tune out the noise by virtue of having so much ownership concentrated his own hands.
claims.speaker: William Thorndike

claims.claim: The Rales brothers at Danaher are cited as a definite fit for the outsider CEO model.
claims.quote: So you mentioned the Rales brothers at Danaher and Colfax. I think they very definitely fit the model.
claims.speaker: William Thorndike

claims.claim: Nick Howley has done an extraordinary job building value at TransDigm, which focuses on specialized aircraft components.
claims.quote: There's a wonderful CEO named Nick Howley who runs a business called TransDigm that focuses on specialized aircraft components. And he's done an extraordinary job building value there.
claims.speaker: William Thorndike

claims.claim: Mark Leonard runs Constellation Software, an interesting Canadian software business, using many outsider principles.
claims.quote: There is a CEO name Mark Leonard who runs a very interesting software business in Canada called Constellation Software using many of these principles.
claims.speaker: William Thorndike

claims.claim: Mike Pearson at Valeant is controversial but has many outsider traits, making it an interesting case to watch unfold.
claims.quote: I believe, controversial as it is at the moment, that Mike Pearson at Valeant, although it's still early days, has many of these traits. And this is a very interesting case to watch unfold.
claims.speaker: William Thorndike

claims.claim: Arch Re is a reinsurer that runs its business very much along the lines of outsider CEOs.
claims.quote: There's a reinsurer called Arch Re that runs its business very much along these lines, I think.
claims.speaker: William Thorndike

claims.claim: Markel Insurance is part of a series of mini Berkshire insurance companies built along similar outsider lines.
claims.quote: There are a series of sort of mini Berkshire insurance companies, Markel Insurance, Fairfax, White Mountains, Allegheny. They are built along similar lines.
claims.speaker: William Thorndike

claims.claim: MVR is a home builder that is cited as a current contemporary example embodying outsider traits very well.
claims.quote: There's a home builder, of all things, called MVR. So I could go on, but there are current, contemporary examples that I think embody these traits very well across a variety of industries.
claims.speaker: William Thorndike

claims.claim: Oracle has been effective in acquisitions which serve as a major channel for capital allocation.
claims.quote: I know that Oracle has been acquisitive over a long period of time. And I believe, although I haven't studied the data, that that's been a very accretive activity for shareholders.
claims.speaker: William Thorndike

claims.claim: Facebook has used internal growth as its primary capital allocation channel, which is a prudent thing to do.
claims.quote: Facebook, it's extraordinary what's gone on in that business. And their primary capital allocation channel has been internal growth. They've been funding internal growth. That's a very prudent thing to do.
claims.speaker: William Thorndike

claims.claim: Google has funded internal growth which has been a great high IRR activity.
claims.quote: That's been true for Google. Impossible to argue that that hasn't been a great high IRR activity for--
claims.speaker: William Thorndike

claims.claim: The YouTube acquisition was a phenomenal acquisition that could be justified.
claims.quote: When you guys did the YouTube acquisition, by the way, it was also a possible to justify it. That's been a phenomenal acquisition.
claims.speaker: William Thorndike

claims.claim: The WhatsApp acquisition seems insane on normal financial metrics but normal metrics may not apply.
claims.quote: I mean, that seems completely insane to me on normal financial metrics, but I don't think normal financial metrics necessarily apply.
claims.speaker: William Thorndike
